tables.title: Notation introduced for the simulation argument

values.Definition: Fraction of all human-level technological civilizations that survive to reach a posthuman stage
Average number of ancestor-simulations run by a posthuman civilization
Average number of individuals that have lived in a civilization before it reaches a posthuman stage

notes: Footnote 10: '100 billion humans × 50 years/human × 30 million secs/year × [10^4, 10^7] operations in each human brain per second ≈ [10^33, 10^36] operations.'

observations: The text introduces a rough estimate of computational power: a planetary-mass computer ≈ 10^42 operations per second, assuming only known nanotechnological designs.
A single such computer could simulate the entire mental history of humankind (an 'ancestor-simulation') using < 1 millionth of its processing power for one second.
A posthuman civilization may build an astronomical number of such computers.
Even allocating only a minute fraction of resources, the available computing power is sufficient to run a huge number of ancestor-simulations.
The conclusion can be drawn even with substantial margin of error in estimates.
Bullet point states: 'Posthuman civilizations would have enough computing power to run hugely many ancestor-simulations even while using only a tiny fraction of their resources for that purpose.'

Section IV introduces the core simulation argument: if there's a substantial chance our civilization reaches posthuman stage and runs many ancestor-simulations, then how are we not living in such a simulation?
Three notation symbols are formally defined: f_P, \overline{N}, \overline{H}.
uncertainties: Estimates are described as 'rough' and may be 'off by several orders of magnitude'.
Assumption of 'only already known nanotechnological designs', which are 'probably far from optimal'.
The argument explicitly allows for 'substantial margin of error in all our estimates'.
The phrase 'even if our estimate is off by several orders of magnitude, this does not matter much for our argument' indicates robustness but also acknowledges uncertainty in quantitative inputs.
